articles.title: Littleborough farm owner seeks permission for wellness retreat with sauna and hot tub
articles.excerpt: Owners of Happy Hideaway in Littleborough have applied for retrospective planning permission to keep their sauna and hot tub retreat on agricultural land.
articles.content_html:
Owners of Happy Hideaway, a wellness retreat at Lower Townhouse Farm on Townhouse Road in Littleborough, have applied to Rochdale Council for retrospective planning permission to retain their facilities, which include a sauna and hot tub.

The retreat, which opened in January 2026, offers a range of wellness treatments designed to help visitors "reconnect, recharge and revive". Facilities include a wood-fired sauna for up to six people, two ice baths, and a wood-fired hot tub for four.

A converted horse box serves as a drinks trailer for guests.

Gemma Wharmby, the owner, stated in the application that Happy Hideaway is a small, wellness-focused sauna business that has received 100% five-star reviews on Google. The application includes plans for the siting of a shipping container, timber sauna, and drinks trailer on the agricultural land.

The outcome of this application will determine whether the wellness retreat can continue operating in its current form, which has been positively received by visitors.

articles.title: Police advice for Rochdale fans after substance forced Co-op Live evacuation during Don Toliver show
articles.excerpt: Anyone who went to Sunday's Don Toliver concert and has since felt unwell should go to hospital, see their GP or call 101, Greater Manchester Police say.
articles.content_html:
Anyone from the Rochdale borough who was at Don Toliver's Co-op Live concert on Sunday night should seek medical help if they have since felt unwell, police say.

Greater Manchester Police said anyone who has noticed side-effects or become unwell since the event should go to their local hospital, contact their GP or call 101.

Officers were alerted by venue staff shortly after 10pm on Sunday 22 November, after reports that people in the crowd were suffering the effects of a substance released near the end of the show.

Police first said the substance was believed to be tear gas. Later updates described it as unknown, and its identity has not been confirmed.

A major incident was declared and more than 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena on the Etihad Campus in east Manchester.

In an update on Monday evening, GMP said 89 people displayed symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure.

One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for assessment and treatment. The other 88 were given dry decontamination at the scene and taken to the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.

The major incident was stood down at 4am on Monday. GMP described the incident as isolated, with no wider threat to the public.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."

Police said enquiries were continuing "to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk". Further testing will be carried out on items found at the venue. No arrests have been made.

Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker, Gold Commander on the night, said the priority had been to "ensure the safety of every person that was attending the concert".

Co-op Live said it was working closely with GMP to identify the cause, and that the safety and security of visitors was its priority.

Don Toliver ended the Manchester show early. His concert at The O2 in London on Monday 23 November has been rescheduled for 15 December, and Live Nation said tickets will be honoured.

Police have not issued a specific public appeal. Anyone with information can contact GMP on 101 or through LiveChat at gmp.police.uk, or report anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111. In an emergency, call 999.

articles.title: Redwood School achieves strong standards in Ofsted inspection
articles.excerpt: Redwood School in Rochdale has received positive feedback from Ofsted, achieving strong standards in five out of seven inspection areas, including inclusion and attendance.
articles.content_html:
Redwood School in Rochdale has received commendations from Ofsted following its latest inspection, achieving strong standards in five out of seven areas assessed. The inspection highlighted the school's effective practices in inclusion and attendance, which are crucial for supporting its diverse student body.

Update, 23 November 2026, 3.09pm: Councillor Rachel Massey commented on the Ofsted report, stating that it is "a fantastic endorsement of the outstanding work taking place across Redwood School."

The school, which caters to children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), met expected standards in both achievement and curriculum. This positive feedback reflects the school's commitment to providing a supportive learning environment for all its pupils.

An Ofsted spokesperson noted that the strong performance in inclusion and attendance demonstrates the school's dedication to fostering an inclusive environment. This is particularly significant as it ensures that all students have the opportunity to thrive academically and socially.

Redwood School's achievements are part of a broader effort within the education sector to enhance standards and support for students with SEND. The school community can look forward to continued improvements and a focus on maintaining these high standards in future inspections.

Wrexham U18s won 1-0 against Preston North End on Saturday, with Oliver McTweed scoring the decisive goal in stoppage time.

The victory is significant for Wrexham's academy, showcasing their ability to score late, a hallmark of their playing style. Carrick Murphy's return from a long-term injury also adds depth to the squad, as noted by Craig Knight, the Professional Development Phase Lead Coach.

Knight praised the importance of late goals, stating that they contribute to the team's success and are part of their football identity. He highlighted that the U18s aim to maintain this trend, which has been influenced by the first team.

Looking ahead, Wrexham U18s are preparing for their next match against Port Vale, where they will look to continue their strong performance and late scoring ability.

articles.title: Heywood's £6 million active travel scheme faces criticism from local councillor
articles.excerpt: A £6 million road and transport scheme in Heywood has drawn criticism from local councillor Mike Howard, who claims it could harm the town.
articles.content_html:
A £6 million road and transport scheme in Heywood has faced significant criticism from local councillor Mike Howard, who argues it could 'destroy the town'.

The scheme, which aims to improve roads, paths, public spaces, and crossing facilities, is set to begin in 2027, according to Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM).

Councillor Howard, representing the Reform UK party, has expressed concerns about the potential negative impacts on local businesses and traffic flow. He has launched an online petition against the scheme, which has already gathered over 200 signatures.

Howard believes that the reduction of access to Hill Street Car Park from Market Street is particularly problematic and reflects a lack of consultation with the community.

The council maintains that there have been two consultations regarding the scheme since it was first proposed in 2024, with over 1,000 residents providing feedback.

TfGM has indicated that adjustments, including the removal of a bus gate on Lance Corporal Stephen Shaw MC Way, were made in response to community input.

As the project moves forward, the council is committed to enhancing public transport facilities along the 471 bus route and installing a new cycle lane. The outcome of the ongoing petition and community feedback may influence the final implementation of the scheme.

Tracey Howarth of Aurora Recovery Limited has been appointed as the liquidator for the winding-up process. The company's registered office is located at 42 Leeds and Bradford Road, Kirkstall, Leeds.

The resolutions were passed as both a special and ordinary resolution, allowing for the voluntary winding-up of the company. This process will involve settling any outstanding debts and distributing any remaining assets to creditors.

The closure of Clover Security Services Ltd may impact local employment and service availability in the Castleton area, as the company has been a provider of security services.

articles.title: You may be able to claim for Turner Brothers asbestos
articles.excerpt: Former workers, their families and people who lived near the Spotland factory can still claim, and there are routes for people exposed elsewhere too.
articles.content_html:
People made ill by asbestos from the former Turner Brothers Asbestos factory in Spotland can still claim compensation, 25 years after the company collapsed.

Former workers can claim, and so can people who never worked there, such as relatives exposed to dust on work clothes and people who lived near the factory.

Claims linked to Turner Brothers are handled by the T&N UK Asbestos Trust, which holds a separate fund for Turner Brothers claims. Its website is tandnasbestos.org.uk.

The trust usually pays a set share of a claim's full value rather than the whole amount.

People exposed to asbestos at other workplaces may also be able to claim, even if their employer closed long ago. Mesothelioma, a cancer caused by asbestos, often takes 40 to 50 years to show symptoms.

An employer's insurer is usually responsible even when the firm no longer exists. The Employers' Liability Tracing Office, at elto.org.uk, helps people find a former employer's insurer, though it does not pay compensation itself.

People diagnosed with mesothelioma who cannot trace a liable employer or insurer may be able to claim from the government's Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme, which pays according to age.

A government lump sum under the Pneumoconiosis etc. (Workers' Compensation) Act 1979 covers certain dust-related diseases when damages cannot be won from an employer, often because it has stopped trading. The claim form helpline is 0800 279 2322.

A separate 2008 mesothelioma scheme covers people exposed through a relative's work clothes, and people who cannot say where they were exposed but were exposed only in the UK.

Since 31 October 2026, dependants claiming under either government scheme after a sufferer died without claiming receive the full amount the sufferer would have been paid.

For a 60-year-old claimant under the 2008 scheme, that raises a dependant's payment from £24,526 to £56,656, according to the government. The change applies to new claims only.

Asbestos products were made at the Spodden Valley site from 1879 until 1998, and it was once the world's largest asbestos textile factory. Turner & Newall went into administration in 2001.

The site's owner, Spodden Park Ltd, began investigation works this month to map where asbestos is buried, ahead of a clean-up and redevelopment.

Compensation claims generally have to begin within three years of diagnosis, or within three years of a death. Some government payments must be claimed within 12 months.

The Greater Manchester Asbestos Victims Support Group, a registered charity, gives free advice on benefits and compensation to people with any asbestos-related disease, and runs support groups for patients and bereaved families.

The group can be contacted on 0161 258 0166, Monday to Friday from 9.30am to 4pm, or at info@gmavsg.org. Specialist asbestos solicitors can advise which routes apply, and many work on a no win, no fee basis.

The management of these services is vital for residents' quality of life, as access to well-maintained libraries and leisure centres supports education and health initiatives within the borough.

As the council continues to oversee these services, residents can expect ongoing improvements and updates regarding local initiatives and community engagement efforts.

articles.title: Free health checks in Rochdale identify 1,000 undiagnosed conditions
articles.excerpt: A community health initiative in Rochdale has revealed that half of participants were unaware they needed medical attention, with 1,000 undiagnosed conditions identified.
articles.content_html:
A community initiative offering free health checks across Rochdale, Heywood, and Middleton has identified 1,000 undiagnosed health conditions among participants. Launched on 31 October 2025, the programme has conducted 2,000 health checks, revealing that 50% of those tested were unaware they needed medical attention.

The Community Health Checks programme, commissioned by Rochdale Council and delivered by the Living Well Rochdale Cardiovascular Disease team, aims to improve access to essential health screenings.

articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has approved plans to turn a house at 9 Thornham New Road, Castleton, into a care home for up to eight adults, with 24-hour care.

The council approved the application on 18 November. The plans include a new upstairs bay window and internal layout changes to the property.

The council received 20 comments on the application. Residents raised concerns about parking, noise and emergency vehicle access to the home.

Highways officers did not object to the application and said the home was unlikely to add much traffic. The driveway has room for three or four cars, and the council requires two parking spaces for a care home of this size.

The applicant says no more than two staff would be on site at once. A planning condition limits the care home to eight residents and requires work to start within three years of approval.

  • The care home is limited to eight residents and must start work within three years of approval.

articles.title: Daalat Ali detained twice during visit to Pakistan amid Kashmir tensions
articles.excerpt: Daalat Ali faced two detentions at Lahore airport during a visit to Pakistan, raising concerns about his safety and the political climate in Kashmir.
articles.content_html:
Daalat Ali, a civic delegation member, was detained twice during a visit to Pakistan, raising concerns about his safety amid ongoing tensions in Kashmir.

His first detention lasted approximately four hours at Lahore airport, where he was questioned before being released after a meeting with the UK High Commissioner.

Ali's second detention occurred when a notification on the airport computer triggered further questioning. He expressed feeling scared during this incident and voiced concerns about not being able to return home safely.

His nephew in Islamabad was reportedly worried for his safety during the visit.

These detentions come in the wake of violent protests in Kashmir, which resulted in the deaths of forty individuals in July.

They later took him to a meeting with the High Commissioner – the UK government’s representative – who let him go. He joined back up with the Rochdale council delegation in Sahiwal – aimed at bringing closer ties between the two towns. ‌ “They didn’t know why they were holding me, “ Coun Ali added. “I went to the immigration desk and something came up on the computer. “We kept asking if I was under arrest and they said no. Coun Ali said: “Coming back, I was advised not to go to Kashmir. But on Monday (November 2) I was told by the High Commissioner’s office I could fly back so I booked my ticket and left.” ‌ Coun Ali ended up staying with a local politician he knew in the country during his extended stay, until he was able to fly home from Islamabad airport on November 4. Rochdale mayor, Coun Faisal Rana, stayed behind with him when he was held again – which Coun Ali ‘was extremely thankful’ for. Although Coun Ali never got answers as to why he was detained, he thinks it was as a result of his previous criticisms of the military administration currently operating in his birthplace of Kashmir. He added that his nephew in Islamabad was worried about hosting him out of fear he would face repercussions from the authorities. ‌ He believes the ordeal is connected to the extremely high political tensions in the Jammu and Kashmir regions of Pakistan at the moment. Law enforcement and protestors were amongst the 40 reportedly killed in July. The JKJAAC were protesting the administration’s handling of the elections for seats in the local assembly, it is understood. The Pakistani government has since proscribed the JKJAAC as a terrorist group, something Amnesty International has described as a violation of freedom rights. ‌ In June, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for South Asia, Isabelle Lassee said: “Branding a grassroots organization as ‘terrorist’ on vague grounds, while simultaneously cutting the region off from the outside world, raises serious concerns regarding the Pakistani authorities’ conduct and their disregard for human rights. “The proscription of JKJAAC under anti-terror laws is disproportionate, unlawful and a violation of the right to freedom of association.” ‌ The Pakistani government also issued new restrictions on international media reporting in the country back on August 5. Pakistan is currently ranked 153th out of 180 on the World Press Freedom Index. According to Reporters Without Borders, Pakistan is one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists, with multiple murders each year that are often linked to cases of corruption or illegal trafficking and which go completely unpunished. ‌ Coun Ali described their regime as ‘oppressive’ and accused them of committing ‘acroticities’ in the area, which is concerning their relatives living in Rochdale and across the UK. “I don’t support oppression at all,” he explained. “I have seen martial law, but this is staunch martial law at its best. ‌ “I know of three families in Rochdale who have had relatives in Kashmir killed. Nothing gets in or out.” ‌ Despite the issues he faced over in the country of his birth, Coun Ali described the actual Rochdale council delegation a success. The mayor was seen cutting the ribbon on a new eye hospital in the area as well as the Sewing Machine Centre by the Al-Mahmood Foundation, established by Humanity Care Relief. The Boarshaw project was awarded to J C Mills & Son Limited for £230,000, while Whittaker Moss's second phase was awarded to W.H. Good Limited for £150,000.

articles.excerpt: Residents are invited to join a free White Ribbon Day vigil walk and service in Rochdale on Wednesday 25 November 2026, commemorating victims of violence and abuse.
articles.content_html:
Residents are invited to join a free White Ribbon Day vigil walk and service in Rochdale on Wednesday 25 November 2026, commemorating victims of violence and abuse.

The council says the walk begins at 5pm outside Number One Riverside on Smith Street, following introductory speeches. Participants will then walk through the town centre to St Mary in the Baum Parish Church on St Mary's Gate.
